title: Stir up the gift (2 Timothy 1:6)
hookLine: Paul tells Timothy to stir up the grace given by the laying on of hands

lines: A HEARTH BANKED FOR THE NIGHT.
A LETTER TO A YOUNG FRIEND.
cards: In a house warmed by an open hearth, the fire was banked at night: ash raked over the last coals, and left. By morning the hearth looked dead.
But brush back the ash, blow gently, add a little kindling, and the flame came back. Paul uses that picture in a letter to Timothy, his young friend and co-worker.
The letter says Paul is writing in chains, and that the time of his own departure is near.

teach.b: He starts with family. He remembers Timothy's faith, which lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. Faith passed down a kitchen table, two generations deep.
Then: "For which cause I admonish thee, that thou stir up the grace of God which is in thee, by the imposition of my hands."
Stir up translates one Greek verb, anazōpyrein: to rekindle, to fan back into flame. Paul isn't telling Timothy to get a new gift. He already has it.
He's telling him not to let it sit under the ash.
Then the next line: "For God hath not given us the spirit of fear: but of power, and of love, and of sobriety." Sobriety here means a sound mind, self-control.
Paul's next words suggest Timothy was timid, and that fear is what banks a fire.

Catholics read the imposition of hands as the sign of ordination. In the sacrament of holy orders, the bishop lays his hands on the head of the one being ordained, in silence, and prays the prayer of consecration.

The Church teaches that ordination marks a person permanently: the gift isn't lost. But it can be neglected, and so can every gift. Catholics speak the same way about the graces of baptism and confirmation.
They were given once, but they need breath. Notice the order: given by God, then stirred up by the person. Paul expects Timothy to do the blowing.

teach.h: STIR UP THE GRACE OF GOD WHICH IS IN THEE.
teach.b: Grace isn't a fire you light alone. But it's also not a fire that tends itself.

how: In the Catholic rite of ordination, the bishop silently lays his hands on the head of each candidate and then prays the prayer of consecration; Catholics also speak of stirring up the graces of baptism and confirmation.

o: to light a brand-new fire from nothing
to put out a fire before it can spread
to rekindle, fanning a gift back into flame

games.q: inside the letter — tap the pairs.

s: Paul tells Timothy to get a new gift
he tells him to rekindle the one already in him.
in Catholic ordination the bishop lays hands on the candidate
in silence, before the prayer of consecration.
Timothy's faith first lived in his grandmother and mother

games.q: you're Timothy. you have a gift from God, but you've grown timid and it's gone dim. what does Paul tell you?
o: stir up the grace that's already in you.
give the work to someone bolder.
games.why: "stir up the grace of God which is in thee": "God hath not given us the spirit of fear."

practice: Think of one gift that's gone quiet under the ash: a way you used to pray, a skill you stopped using, a patience or courage you once had.

Picture it as a coal, still warm, and picture blowing on it gently: what's one small piece of kindling, ten minutes, a call, a page? If you pray, ask for help to stir it up; if not, simply choose the kindling.

wordCard.voice: Anazopyrein, to rekindle. Paul's word to Timothy: fan back into flame the grace given by the laying on of hands. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: to rekindle, to fan into flame (2 Timothy 1:6).

carryVoice: Your line: fanned back into flame. And that's week eighty-five: rejoice always, arete, content, syndesmos, adialeiptos, koimaomai, and anazopyrein. Day five hundred ninety-five, done.
